questions.question: Caliph Umar II (Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, r. 717–720) implemented major fiscal and social administrative reforms regarding non-Arab converts to Islam (mawali). What was the primary financial component of this reform, and what was its broader administrative impact?
options: He exempted mawali from paying the jizya (poll tax) upon conversion, creating a fiscal deficit that forced subsequent Umayyad rulers to reverse the policy.
He doubled the kharaj (land tax) on Arab landowners to subsidize non-Arab converts, triggering a mutiny among the Syrian garrison troops.
He mandated that all mawali be enrolled in the regular military register (diwan) with full pensions, which bankrupted the imperial treasury.
He nationalized agricultural land held by mawali in Khurasan, directly inciting the immediate outbreak of the Abbasid Revolution.

questions.question: In the administrative structure of the Vijayanagara Empire (14th–16th centuries), the Nayankara system served as a key mechanism of provincial governance. What was the defining feature of this system?
options: Provincial governors were elected annually by merchant guilds (nagaram) to oversee urban commerce and maritime customs.
Military commanders (Nayakas) were granted territorial fiefs (amaram) in exchange for maintaining military contingents and remitting annual tribute to the sovereign.
Hereditary Brahmin tax-collectors managed rural agrarian output without military duties or fiscal obligations to the central court.
Foreign mercenaries were awarded monopolies over local ports in exchange for enforcing royal legal decrees along the coast.

questions.question: During the White Lotus Rebellion (1796–1804) against the Qing Dynasty, traditional imperial military forces such as the Eight Banners proved largely ineffective against the insurgent guerrilla tactics. What primary strategy allowed the Qing court to eventually suppress the rebellion?
options: Deploying European-trained expeditionary forces armed with modern rifled artillery.
Privatizing provincial mints to finance permanent foreign mercenary corps.
Combining a policy of 'clearing the countryside and strengthening the walls' with the deployment of locally raised peasant militias (tuanlian).
Enacting widespread agrarian land redistribution that satisfied White Lotus socio-economic demands.

questions.question: During the conflict between Xhosa chiefdoms and British colonial expansion in southern Africa, the disastrous Cattle-Killing Movement of 1856–1857 decimated the Xhosa population. What was the principal motivation driving this event?
options: A tactical scorched-earth policy executed by Xhosa chiefs to deprive advancing British forces of local provisions.
A imperial mandate from British colonial authorities requiring the slaughter of all livestock to contain a rinderpest outbreak.
A millenarian conversion effort designed to adapt Xhosa traditions to Dutch Calvinism in order to form an anti-British alliance.
Prophecies articulated by Nongqawuse asserting that destroying livestock and crops would cause ancestral spirits to rise and expel the British.

questions.question: The Zanj Rebellion (869–883 CE) posed one of the most severe internal threats to the Abbasid Caliphate during the late 9th century. What was the social background and geographic epicenter of this revolt?
options: Enslaved East Africans working under harsh conditions in the salt marshes and agricultural drainage projects of lower Mesopotamia.
Persian silk artisans revolting against state-imposed price controls and monopolies in the urban center of Isfahan.
Bedouin tribal confederations demanding the restoration of lost grazing privileges throughout the central Hijaz.
Nubian river traders protesting restrictive Abbasid tariffs along the trade routes of Upper Egypt.
